newsitem.title: USA: U.S., N. Korea hold fresh talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S., N. Korea hold fresh talks.

text.p: The United States and North Korea on Tuesday held new talks on establishing liaison offices in each other's capitals and recovering remains of U.S. servicemen lost in the Korean War, the State Department said.
"The discussions today were useful in further clarifying views on these issues," the department said in a statement.
Before the talks, department spokesman Nicholas Burns discounted South Korean news reports that the two sides had reached agreement on setting up the long-delayed offices.
"We have not reached an agreement with the North Korean government to establish by a date certain the liaison offices," he told reporters.

"The ultimate agreement to establish the liaison offices is obviously going to be part of a broader picture ... a function of the development of relations between South Korea and North Korea," he said.

The North Korean delegation, after participating in a ground-breaking U.S.-South Korean briefing in New York on a Washington-Seoul proposal for Korean peninsula peace talks, came to Washington as guests of the Atlantic Council, a thinktank specialising in NATO affairs.

But Burns said members of the delegation, including the deputy director of the American Affairs Bureau in the North Korean Foreign Ministry, also met Tuesday with Mark Minton, director of the State Department's office of Korean affairs.
Unlike the talks last week in New York, however, the discussions at the State Department involved working level, not senior level, officials.
The State Department said the discussion focused on bilateral issues, including joint efforts to recover the remains of U.S. Korean War soldiers, non-proliferation concerns and liaison offices.

The United States and North Korea do not have formal diplomatic relations but have been in regular contact since the two signed a 1994 landmark nuclear deal in which Pyongyang agreed to halt its nuclear programme in return for $5 billion in new nuclear power reactors and alternate energy supplies.
U.S. officials have said the two sides must still resolve technical issues concerning the liaison offices, including purchasing office space and observing city and federal regulations.

The officials have also said they have been unable to reach agreement so far with Pyongyang on how a U.S. office in the North Korean capital would be resupplied overland across the Korean demilitarized zone.

But Burns made clear that such technical issues are really ancillary. "If relations between South Korea and North Korea do not proceed -- in fact, if they recede -- then there are going to be problems in the U.S.-North Korean relationship," he said.
